exercises.title: Backstage & IDP Vocabulary
exercises.subtitle: 5 exercises - practice the vocabulary for Backstage, internal developer portals, catalog entity kinds, TechDocs, and software templates.

questions.q: A colleague says: "We registered our payment service in Backstage." What does this mean?
options: A catalog-info.yaml descriptor was added to the service repository and Backstage has discovered and indexed it in the software catalog.
The service was deployed to production and is now monitored by Backstage.
The service's API was published to an external developer portal for third-party consumption.
The service was granted elevated permissions in the Backstage identity provider.
questions.explanation: Registration in Backstage means adding a catalog-info.yaml file to a repository and letting Backstage's catalog ingestion discover it. Once indexed, the component appears in the software catalog with its owner, lifecycle stage, dependencies, and documentation link. It has nothing to do with deployment or permissions.

questions.q: In a catalog-info.yaml file, which kind would you use for a team's deployed microservice?
options: kind: Component - it describes a software piece like a microservice, library, or website
kind: Resource - because the microservice consumes cloud resources
kind: API - because the microservice exposes an API
kind: System - because a microservice is a system-level concern
questions.explanation: kind: Component is the correct entity type for a deployable unit like a microservice, frontend app, or library. kind: API describes the API contract itself (OpenAPI, gRPC). kind: System groups multiple components into a logical system. kind: Resource describes infrastructure (databases, S3 buckets). Getting these kinds right is essential for accurate catalog modelling.

questions.q: Complete the sentence your tech lead uses in a platform review: "Instead of writing boilerplate manually, developers use a _____ template in Backstage to scaffold a new service - it creates the repository, sets up CI, and registers the component automatically."
options: software
catalog
deployment
infrastructure
questions.explanation: Software templates (previously called the Scaffolder) are a core Backstage feature. They encode platform team best practices into self-service forms. A developer picks a template (e.g., "New Node.js microservice"), fills in name/owner/team, and Backstage automates everything downstream. This is how IDPs reduce "day zero" friction.

questions.q: Your platform team says: "We use TechDocs to keep documentation close to the code." What approach does TechDocs follow?
options: It generates API reference docs from OpenAPI specs and hosts them on a CDN.
It uses AI to generate documentation from code comments and Git commit messages.
It follows a docs-as-code approach - Markdown files live in the service repository and are rendered in Backstage alongside the catalog entry.
It imports Confluence pages into Backstage and keeps them in sync via webhooks.
questions.explanation: TechDocs implements the docs-as-code philosophy: Markdown files (using MkDocs) live next to the service code in the same repository. Backstage builds and serves them as a unified documentation site. When you open a catalog component, you see its docs tab alongside the API, dependencies, and CI status - everything in one place.

questions.q: A developer asks: "Who owns this service?" and checks the Backstage catalog. Which field in catalog-info.yaml answers this question?
options: spec.lifecycle
spec.type
metadata.tags
spec.owner
questions.explanation: spec.owner defines the team or individual responsible for the component - typically a reference to a kind: Group entity (e.g., team-payments ). This is the field that answers "who do I contact if this service is down?" and drives accountability. spec.lifecycle describes the stage (production, experimental, deprecated). spec.type describes what kind of component it is (service, library, website).

questions.q: Sarah : "Hey team, I'm using the IDP to automatically provision a new database instance for my service. It's much faster than manually setting it up!" What does Sarah mean when she mentions using the IDP (Infrastructure Delivery Platform)?
options: It describes a system that automatically manages and deploys infrastructure resources based on defined service requirements.
It's the name of the internal Slack channel for infrastructure requests.
It refers to a specific, custom-built tool within our development workflow.
It's a type of code editor used by developers to create database instances.
questions.explanation: Sarah is referring to an Infrastructure Delivery Platform (IDP), which is a system designed to automate the provisioning and management of infrastructure - in this case, a database instance. IDPs streamline development by removing manual steps, ensuring consistency, and reducing errors. The key here is that it's about *automation* and connecting software requests directly to underlying resources, not just a tool or communication channel.

questions.q: David : "I've submitted a PR to update the API endpoint for our user authentication service. It's currently using the legacy v1 endpoint; we need to migrate to v2 for improved security and performance." Which of the following best describes David's comment within the context of Backstage and IDP?
options: It highlights the importance of maintaining compatibility with older versions of the API, suggesting a need for backward-compatible changes within the service itself.
It refers to a manual deployment process managed outside of Backstage, requiring David to trigger a separate release pipeline.
It indicates that David is requesting the IDP to automatically update the service's configuration to utilize the new v2 endpoint and potentially handle any necessary routing or DNS updates.
It's a request for a code review focusing solely on the security vulnerabilities associated with the legacy v1 endpoint, without mentioning infrastructure changes.
questions.explanation: David is describing a situation where the IDP (Infrastructure Delivery Platform) can automatically update the service's configuration. The core of his comment - migrating to v2 - directly relates to the IDP's role in managing and deploying services, including updating API endpoints. Options B and A misrepresent the IDP's capabilities; it doesn't simply trigger deployments or focus solely on security reviews. Option C accurately reflects how the IDP would handle this update.

questions.q: Mark just posted a PR updating the deployment configuration for his new service in Backstage. The PR includes a comment: 'IDP is automating the creation of our Kubernetes manifests and deploying this service to production.' Considering Mark's comment, and knowing that Backstage integrates with an IDP, what does Mark *primarily* mean by mentioning the IDP? Hint: Think about how IDPs typically streamline deployment workflows.
questions.explanation: Mark means that the Infrastructure Delivery Platform (IDP) is automating a significant part of the deployment workflow. While Backstage provides a central catalog and management interface, the IDP handles the actual creation of infrastructure components like Kubernetes manifests - this reduces manual effort and potential errors. The incorrect options oversimplify the IDP's role; it's not just about provisioning or monitoring, but orchestrating the entire process from code commit to production deployment.

exercises.title: Developer Portal Adoption Metrics
exercises.subtitle: 5 exercises - practice the vocabulary for portal adoption metrics: active users, time to first commit, ROI, and developer satisfaction.

questions.q: A platform team presents this metric: "Monthly active users of the developer portal: 142 out of 180 engineers." What does active users mean in this context?
options: Engineers who have logged into the portal and performed at least one meaningful action (search, view, scaffold) in the past 30 days.
Engineers who have submitted a feature request or bug report through the portal in the past month.
Engineers who have been granted admin access to manage catalog entries.
All engineers who have a portal account, whether they used it recently or not.
questions.explanation: Active users is a standard product metric counting users who interact meaningfully within a time window - typically monthly (MAU) or weekly (WAU). For a developer portal, "meaningful action" means searching the catalog, viewing a service page, running a software template, or accessing TechDocs. Simply having an account does not count. 142/180 = 79% MAU is a strong adoption signal.

questions.q: A CTO asks the platform team: "What is our time to find service owner?" What does this metric measure?
options: The SLA for responding to ownership change requests submitted through the portal.
The average time it takes an engineer to locate the responsible team or person for a given service - using the developer portal or any other means.
The average time between a service incident and the owner being paged via PagerDuty.
The time required to assign an owner to a newly registered service in the catalog.
questions.explanation: Time to find service owner is a key developer portal ROI metric. Without a portal, finding who owns a service might require Slack messages, wiki searches, or asking around - averaging 10-20 minutes. With a well-maintained catalog, it should take under 30 seconds. Reducing this time has a direct impact on incident resolution speed and cross-team collaboration efficiency.

questions.q: Complete the sentence from a platform team quarterly review: "After launching the self-service scaffolding feature, our _____ decreased from 3 days to 4 hours - new engineers can now have their first commit in the same day they join the team."
options: onboarding completion rate
time to first commit
deployment frequency
lead time for changes
questions.explanation: Time to first commit is a developer onboarding metric that measures how long it takes a new engineer to make their first meaningful contribution. It is a powerful proxy for onboarding effectiveness and developer experience. A portal with software templates, clear documentation, and a software catalog dramatically reduces this time by eliminating the "where do I start?" problem.

questions.q: Your platform team wants to make the business case for investing in the developer portal. Which statement best articulates portal ROI ?
options: "The portal generates revenue directly by allowing external partners to discover our internal APIs."

"By reducing time spent searching for service owners, onboarding new engineers, and duplicating work across teams, the portal saves an estimated 2 hours per engineer per week - translating to significant productivity gains at scale."
"The portal reduces our cloud infrastructure costs by consolidating services onto fewer nodes."
"The portal improves our security posture by enforcing RBAC policies on all catalog entries."
questions.explanation: Portal ROI is best expressed as time savings multiplied by headcount. The most common value drivers are: (1) faster service discovery - less time paging people on Slack; (2) faster onboarding - new engineers productive sooner; (3) reduced duplication - teams can find existing services before building new ones; (4) faster incident resolution - ownership is immediately clear. Quantify these in engineering hours to make the business case.

questions.q: A platform manager says: "Our developer satisfaction survey scores for the portal dropped from 4.1 to 3.4 this quarter." How should this be interpreted?
options: Developer satisfaction with the portal has declined, suggesting friction, missing features, or quality issues that warrant investigation through follow-up questions or user interviews.
The portal had a major outage this quarter, causing the score to drop.
The score drop indicates fewer engineers are using the portal, not lower satisfaction.
The survey methodology changed, making the scores incomparable across quarters.
questions.explanation: Developer satisfaction surveys (often using a Likert scale or eNPS-style question like "How satisfied are you with the developer portal?") are a leading indicator of portal health. A drop from 4.1 to 3.4 is a significant signal. The right response is to investigate: run follow-up questions, conduct user interviews, or analyse which features correlate with lower ratings. Platform teams use this data to prioritise the product roadmap.

questions.q: PR Description Subject: Refactor User Authentication Flow @johndoe Please review. This PR streamlines the user authentication flow by migrating to a centralized token management system. We've also added logging for all authentication attempts, which should help with debugging and monitoring. (This is a comment left on a Pull Request in our code repository.) What does the phrase 'centralized token management system' most likely refer to within this context?
options: D: A new library that automatically handles OAuth 2.0 authentication flows.
B: A single, secure service responsible for generating, validating, and managing developer API tokens.
A: A database containing all user passwords encrypted using AES-256.
C: The team's internal documentation outlining best practices for password security.
questions.explanation: This question tests understanding of a common developer portal term. 'Centralized token management system' refers to a single place where the portal manages and controls access for developers - essentially, it's not each application needing its own individual authentication process. Option C is incorrect because password storage typically involves much more than just AES-256 encryption; options D and A are related but don't represent the core functionality described in the PR comment. The key here is recognizing that 'token management' implies a system for controlling access, not just storing passwords.

questions.q: During a standup meeting, Sarah (Platform Team) says: 'Our developer portal adoption rate is trending positively - we've seen a 20% increase in daily active users over the last week.' What does 'daily active users' primarily represent in this context?
questions.explanation: 'Daily active users' refers to the number of *unique* developers who accessed the portal on a given day. It's crucial to distinguish this from 'total users,' which would include accounts that might be inactive or have only logged in briefly. Using 'daily' provides a clearer picture of ongoing engagement.

questions.q: You receive an API response from the developer portal analytics service: { "endpoint_usage": { "new_user_registrations": 1250, "documentation_views": 7890 }, "developer_engagement": { "active_developers": 345, "average_session_duration": 60} } Which of the following best summarizes the key insights from this API data regarding developer engagement?
questions.explanation: This API response provides core engagement metrics: the number of 'active developers,' which is a key indicator of portal adoption, and their 'average session duration,' indicating how long developers spend utilizing the platform. This combination offers a holistic view of developer interaction.

questions.q: Mark (Engineering Manager) comments on a PR: 'This change significantly reduces the number of support tickets related to API key management. It's a good step towards simplifying the developer experience.' What is Mark primarily evaluating in this comment?
questions.explanation: Mark is assessing the *impact* of the PR - specifically, its effect on developer workflows. Reducing support tickets directly relates to improved developer productivity and a smoother experience, which are vital metrics for portal adoption. The technical aspects of the code itself are secondary to this outcome.

questions.q: During a discussion about developer portal metrics, David (Product Manager) states: 'We need to track the number of developers successfully deploying new features using our CI/CD pipeline integration.' What is the primary purpose of this metric?
questions.explanation: This metric - successful deployments via CI/CD integration - directly reflects the portal's value in streamlining the development lifecycle. Tracking this allows you to gauge how effectively developers are utilizing the portal's capabilities for feature delivery and adoption; it's a critical measure of its ROI.

questions.q: You're reviewing a Slack message from a developer: 'Portal search is still awful! I spent 20 minutes trying to find the documentation for the generate_report function.' What does this feedback highlight about the portal's usability?
questions.explanation: This feedback directly points to a usability issue - poor search functionality. A significant time investment (20 minutes) searching for documentation indicates a core problem that needs addressing. This highlights the importance of tracking metrics related to portal efficiency and developer satisfaction.

exercises.title: Developer Portal Metrics Vocabulary
exercises.subtitle: Practice English vocabulary for measuring developer portal success: catalog completeness, onboarding time, time to first commit, template usage rate, self-service ratio, and portal NPS.

questions.q: What does 'time to first commit for a new hire' measure in a developer portal context?
options: The average time between a developer's first commit and the first code review comment

The elapsed time from a new engineer's start date to when they make their first merged commit - a proxy for how fast the onboarding experience and self-service tooling enable a new hire to become productive
The number of days before a new employee's laptop is fully configured with developer tools
The time it takes a junior developer to submit their first pull request after completing onboarding training
questions.explanation: 'Time to first commit' (or 'time to first PR') is a widely used developer experience metric. A portal with good templates, clear documentation, and self-service setup reduces this from weeks to days. Tracking it shows whether portal investments actually improve onboarding.

questions.q: What is the 'self-service ratio' in developer portal metrics?
options: The percentage of developers who prefer self-service documentation over team training

The proportion of developer tasks (creating services, provisioning environments, onboarding, etc.) completed through the portal's self-service workflows versus those requiring manual intervention from the platform team
The ratio of portal page views to total engineering headcount
The number of catalog-registered services divided by the total estimated number of services in production
questions.explanation: Self-service ratio measures portal effectiveness: if 80% of environment provisioning requests are fulfilled through the portal without a platform team ticket, that is an 80% self-service ratio. Increasing this ratio is a key goal - it reduces platform team toil and unblocks developers.

questions.q: How would you explain 'template usage rate' as a portal health metric?
options: The percentage of Backstage software templates that have been reviewed and approved by the architecture review board

The proportion of new services or components created using the portal's scaffolding templates rather than being set up manually - high usage indicates teams trust and adopt the platform's golden paths
The number of template pull requests merged per sprint across all engineering teams
The ratio of template downloads to total portal page views in a given month
questions.explanation: Template usage rate tells you whether engineers actually use the paved road or bypass it. Low usage means templates are either hard to find, don't meet team needs, or lack trust. High usage means the platform team's investment in templates is paying off.

questions.q: What is 'developer portal NPS' and what does it indicate?
options: Net Provisioning Score - how many services were provisioned through the portal in the last quarter
Net Promoter Score applied to the developer portal - it measures whether engineers would recommend the portal to colleagues, used as a proxy for overall developer experience satisfaction
Net Performance Score - the latency and uptime SLA of the portal itself
New Platform Score - a composite metric of catalog completeness, template coverage, and onboarding time
questions.explanation: Developer NPS (or DevEx NPS) asks engineers: 'How likely are you to recommend this portal to a colleague?' on a 0-10 scale. Promoters (9-10) minus Detractors (0-6) gives the NPS. It is a leading indicator of portal adoption and developer satisfaction, though it must be paired with qualitative feedback.

questions.q: An engineering leader says 'our onboarding time reduction KPI is at 40%'. What does this mean?
options: 40% of new engineers complete onboarding in under 40 hours
The average time from a new hire's start date to full productivity has decreased by 40% since the developer portal was introduced - for example, from 10 days to 6 days
40% of onboarding steps have been automated in the portal compared to the previous manual process
The portal's onboarding section has a 40% completion rate among new joiners
questions.explanation: Onboarding time reduction is measured as a percentage improvement: (old_time - new_time) / old_time × 100. A 40% reduction is a strong signal that the portal's templates, documentation, and self-service setup are materially speeding up new hire productivity.

questions.q: Code Review Comment During a code review of the new payment integration API, Sarah comments: 'The response time for this endpoint is consistently high - >500ms. We need to investigate further and track the average latency across multiple requests.' What does Sarah *actually* mean when she uses the term 'average latency' in this context? Consider the goal of a developer portal regarding API performance.
options: A: The total time it takes for one single request to complete, regardless of how many other requests are running concurrently.

B: A statistical measure representing the typical delay experienced by users when accessing the API endpoint; it's calculated by averaging the response times across multiple requests under similar conditions.
C: The maximum possible response time allowed by the API specification, ensuring all operations complete within a defined timeframe.
D: The number of milliseconds required for the server to process the request before sending the first byte of data back to the client.
questions.explanation: Sarah is referring to *average latency*, which is a crucial metric in developer portal health. This represents the typical delay experienced by developers when accessing the API endpoint-it's calculated by averaging response times across multiple requests. The goal of the portal is to minimize this latency, ensuring responsive APIs and a smooth development experience. Option A is incorrect because it refers to *response time*, not average latency; option C focuses on a maximum limit, while option D describes a specific part of the process.

The percentage of developers using the approved, standardized code templates for authentication and other common tasks.
The frequency with which developers are requesting access to legacy APIs.
A measure of developer satisfaction with existing documentation.
questions.explanation: John is referring to a key portal metric - 'template usage rate' - which indicates how effectively developers are utilizing pre-built solutions and approved patterns. This isn't simply about the number of endpoints created; it reflects whether developers are adhering to established standards, reducing redundancy, and streamlining development efforts. Tracking this helps identify areas where resources (documentation, training) need adjustment to improve developer productivity and portal health.

exercises.title: Golden Paths & Paved Roads Vocabulary
exercises.subtitle: Practice English vocabulary for golden paths, paved roads, and developer experience in internal developer portals: opinionated workflows, self-service, guardrails, and platform adoption language.

questions.q: What is a 'golden path' in the context of an Internal Developer Portal?
options: The production deployment pipeline for critical services

A pre-approved, opinionated set of tools, templates, and workflows that the platform team recommends developers follow to build and deploy services - designed to reduce cognitive load and encode best practices
A visual dashboard showing the most popular API routes
A security scanning workflow triggered before each release
questions.explanation: A golden path (also called a paved road) is the platform team's curated 'happy path' through the complexity of building software. By choosing the golden path, developers get pre-configured CI/CD, security scanning, observability, and deployment - without needing to assemble these themselves. The name implies there are other paths, but the golden one is the recommended route.

questions.q: A platform engineer says: 'We want to reduce cognitive load for developers.' In a developer portal context, what does this mean?
options: We want developers to attend fewer meetings

We want to reduce the mental effort developers spend on infrastructure, security, and tooling choices - so they can focus on writing product features. The portal achieves this by providing self-service templates, pre-configured environments, and automated guardrails
We want to simplify the portal's visual design
We want to limit the number of programming languages teams can use
questions.explanation: Cognitive load is a key concept in developer experience (DevEx). Platform teams use portals to remove 'accidental complexity' - the effort of stitching together infrastructure, choosing tools, and configuring pipelines. When developers follow the golden path, they get all of this automatically, freeing mental bandwidth for solving business problems.

questions.q: What does it mean when a platform team says a workflow has 'guardrails'?
options: The workflow has been reviewed by the legal and compliance team

Automated checks and constraints are built into the process - for example, preventing deployment without security scans, enforcing naming conventions, or blocking access to unapproved dependencies - so developers can move fast without accidentally violating policies
A physical safety review has been completed
The workflow requires two approvals before merging
questions.explanation: Guardrails are automated policy enforcement mechanisms built into the platform. Unlike gates (which block progress), guardrails guide developers in the right direction - for example, linting, SAST scanning, or policy-as-code checks that run automatically. The term implies: you can still move freely, but the platform prevents you from going off the edge.

questions.q: The portal documentation says: 'Provision a new service using our self-service templates.' What does 'provision' mean here?
options: To write the source code for a new service

To create and configure all the infrastructure, repositories, CI pipelines, monitoring, and catalog entries needed for a new service - automatically, through the portal, without raising a ticket to another team
To approve a purchase order for cloud resources
To add documentation to the existing service
questions.explanation: In platform engineering, 'provisioning' means creating and configuring the full set of resources a service needs to exist: a Git repository, CI/CD pipeline, cloud infrastructure, monitoring dashboards, and catalog registration. Self-service provisioning via templates is a core promise of developer portals - it replaces the traditional model where a developer would email an ops team and wait.

questions.q: A senior platform engineer says: 'We need better platform adoption.' What are they likely concerned about?
options: The platform team needs to hire more engineers

Developers are not using the portal's golden paths, templates, and self-service capabilities - instead using ad-hoc, inconsistent approaches. Improving adoption means making the portal more useful, discoverable, and frictionless so developers choose the platform over rolling their own solutions
The platform needs to support more programming languages
The portal's uptime metrics are below SLA
questions.explanation: Platform adoption measures how many teams and services use the platform's capabilities versus going off-platform. Low adoption often means the golden path has too much friction, doesn't support the teams' tech stack, or developers aren't aware of what the portal offers. Platform teams track adoption through metrics like 'percentage of services using the catalog' or 'percentage of deployments via approved pipelines'.

options: It suggests a completely new, bespoke authentication system was built from scratch.
It indicates that the PR is focused on optimizing existing workflows for efficiency and ease of use, aligning with established best practices.
The term 'Golden Path' implies a complex, highly customized onboarding process involving several undocumented steps.
This description incorrectly uses 'Golden Path'; it should have simply stated that the PR implements the new user onboarding flow.
questions.explanation: The correct answer highlights the core concept of the 'Golden Path': leveraging existing, well-defined processes to simplify tasks. The PR's description correctly identifies that it's streamlining an onboarding process by utilizing established services - a classic example of following the paved road. The Golden Path is a deliberately complex series of steps created to ensure all users experience every feature of the platform, regardless of their needs.

The Golden Path refers to the most efficient and commonly used sequence of actions for new users to complete key tasks - essentially, the 'best' way to onboard them. It's about reducing friction and guiding users towards successful adoption.

exercises.title: Platform Maturity & DevEx Vocabulary
exercises.subtitle: Practice English vocabulary for platform maturity models, developer experience metrics, DORA metrics, and platform team communication in developer portals.

questions.q: What do DORA metrics measure in the context of platform engineering?
options: The uptime of the developer portal itself

Four key engineering performance indicators: Deployment Frequency (how often you deploy), Lead Time for Changes (how long from commit to production), Change Failure Rate (how often a change causes an incident), and Mean Time to Recovery (how quickly you recover from failures)
The number of developers using the internal platform
API response times and error rates in production
questions.explanation: DORA (DevOps Research and Assessment) metrics are the industry-standard way to measure software delivery performance. Platform teams use them to demonstrate the impact of their work: a well-designed golden path typically improves Deployment Frequency and Lead Time for Changes while reducing Change Failure Rate. Teams are classified as Elite, High, Medium, or Low performers based on these metrics.

questions.q: A platform team says they are 'at level 2 of the platform maturity model.' What does this indicate?
options: They have built exactly two internal tools

The platform has progressed beyond ad-hoc tooling and has some standardised, self-service capabilities, but has not yet achieved full product-quality developer experience with comprehensive documentation, SLOs, and measured adoption
They have two full-time platform engineers
The platform supports two programming language ecosystems
questions.explanation: Platform maturity models (such as those from Gartner or the CNCF Platforms whitepaper) typically describe a progression from reactive/ad-hoc tooling to a product-managed internal platform with clear SLOs, a roadmap, and measurable DevEx impact. Level 2 usually means the platform exists as a defined capability with some self-service features, but is not yet treated as a first-class product with a developer-facing roadmap and formal adoption metrics.

questions.q: What does 'time to first deployment' (TTFD) measure as a DevEx metric?
options: How long it takes to fix a failed deployment
How long it takes a new developer or team to go from zero to having their first successful deployment through the platform - a measure of onboarding efficiency and golden path quality
The time between writing code and a CI pipeline completing
The average deployment duration across all services
questions.explanation: Time to First Deployment is a key developer experience metric for platform teams. It measures the onboarding journey: from a developer's first day (or a team starting a new service) to their first successful production deployment. A short TTFD indicates that the platform's golden path, documentation, and self-service templates are working well. Long TTFDs signal friction in the onboarding process.

questions.q: The platform roadmap includes 'reducing toil for application teams.' What does 'toil' mean in this context?
options: Unpleasant interpersonal conflicts within engineering teams

Manual, repetitive, automatable work that grows linearly with service count - such as manually updating dependencies, provisioning environments, or rotating secrets - that platform tooling should eliminate
Slow CI/CD pipelines that make developers wait
Complex code reviews that require expert knowledge
questions.explanation: 'Toil' is a term popularised by Google's SRE book. It refers to work that is manual, repetitive, automatable, devoid of lasting value, and scales linearly with traffic or service count. Platform engineering's core value proposition is reducing application team toil - replacing manual environment provisioning, secret rotation, certificate management, and dependency updates with automated platform capabilities.

questions.q: A platform team says they are 'treating the platform as a product.' What does this mean?
options: The platform is being sold to external customers

The platform team operates like a product team: they have a roadmap, conduct developer research (e.g., surveys, interviews), maintain a backlog prioritised by developer impact, publish documentation, maintain SLOs for platform services, and measure adoption - rather than building tools reactively in response to requests
The platform has a commercial licence and requires approval to use
The platform team reports to the product management department
questions.explanation: 'Platform as a product' is a core principle in modern platform engineering. It shifts the team's mindset from 'we build tools when asked' to 'we run a product with internal customers (development teams)'. This means: understanding developer needs through research, measuring satisfaction (e.g., via developer NPS), maintaining a public roadmap, providing documentation and onboarding guides, and defining SLOs so teams can rely on the platform.

questions.q: Sarah : 'Hey team, I'm seeing a huge spike in error rates from the user authentication service. The API response times are consistently above 500ms and we're getting a lot of 'connection refused' errors. It's impacting user login flows significantly.' Mark (a Platform Engineer) replies: 'Okay, I'm investigating . We need to look at the platform maturity around authentication - specifically, is our service observability robust enough? Are we leveraging caching effectively?'
options: The team should immediately roll back the last deployment to address the immediate error rate.
'Observability' refers solely to adding more logging statements; a simple log level change will solve the problem.

'Observability' encompasses metrics, logs, and traces - providing insights into system behavior to proactively identify and resolve issues like this one. It's key to understanding DevEx when things break.
The team should focus on reducing the number of API calls made by the authentication service to improve performance.
questions.explanation: This scenario highlights the importance of 'observability' in platform maturity and DevEx. While reducing API calls might be a tactic later, initially, understanding *why* the response times are high is crucial. Observability-metrics, logs, and traces-is about proactively detecting problems like this before they significantly impact user experience. Option A suggests an immediate rollback without investigation; Option B misunderstands the scope of observability, and Option D doesn't address the root cause.

questions.q: PR Description: "Fix: Improved error handling for user profile updates. Added retry logic with exponential backoff. Monitoring now alerts on failed updates." During a code review discussion, your team lead asks you to elaborate on the 'exponential backoff' mentioned in the PR description. Which of the following best explains this term within the context of improving Developer Experience (DevEx)?
questions.explanation: Exponential backoff is a crucial DevEx element because it intelligently handles transient failures - like network hiccups or temporary service unavailability. Instead of blindly retrying immediately (which could exacerbate the problem), the system increases the delay between each retry exponentially (e.g., 1s, 2s, 4s, 8s...), giving the failing service time to recover. This prevents overwhelming a struggling service and significantly improves resilience - a key aspect of a mature platform that minimizes friction for developers.

Are we leveraging caching effectively?'
options: The team should immediately roll back the last deployment to address the immediate error rate.

Which of the following best explains this term within the context of improving Developer Experience (DevEx)?
questions.explanation: Exponential backoff is a crucial DevEx element because it intelligently handles transient failures - like network hiccups or temporary service unavailability. Instead of blindly retrying immediately (which could exacerbate the problem), the system increases the delay between each retry exponentially (e.g., 1s, 2s, 4s, 8s...), giving the failing service time to recover. Percentage of Successful Transactions

exercises.subtitle: Practice English vocabulary for Team Topologies: platform team, stream-aligned team, enabling team, cognitive load reduction, golden path, paved road, and 'you build it you run it'.

questions.q: In the Team Topologies model, what is a 'stream-aligned team'?
options: A team that manages data streaming infrastructure like Kafka and Kinesis

A team aligned to a continuous flow of work from a segment of the business domain - such as a product area or customer journey - with end-to-end responsibility from feature development to production operations
A team that synchronises releases across multiple product lines on a shared sprint schedule
A team responsible for maintaining alignment between engineering and business strategy documents
questions.explanation: Stream-aligned teams are the primary team type in Team Topologies - they deliver value directly. They own a slice of the product end-to-end and interact with platform, enabling, and complicated-subsystem teams to reduce cognitive load and stay focused on their domain.

questions.q: What is the purpose of a 'platform team' in the Team Topologies model?
options: To manage cloud vendor relationships and negotiate enterprise licensing agreements

To provide self-service internal services, tools, and capabilities that stream-aligned teams can use autonomously - reducing the cognitive load on product teams by abstracting away infrastructure complexity
To review and approve all architecture decisions made by product engineering teams
To maintain the organisation's technology radar and publish quarterly blip updates
questions.explanation: The platform team's product is the internal platform - a curated set of services, APIs, and tooling that stream-aligned teams consume without needing to understand the underlying complexity. The platform team measures success by adoption and developer satisfaction, not just availability.

questions.q: What does 'cognitive load reduction' mean as a platform team goal?
options: Reducing the number of programming languages engineers must know by standardising the stack

Decreasing the amount of irrelevant or complex information a stream-aligned team must hold in mind to do their core work - by abstracting infrastructure details, providing sensible defaults, and building self-service tooling
Reducing the number of meetings engineers attend each week by automating status reporting
Limiting the size of engineering teams to ensure each team can communicate without coordination overhead
questions.explanation: Cognitive load reduction is a central Theme Topologies concept. Every operational concern a platform team absorbs (CI setup, security scanning, log aggregation) is cognitive load removed from stream-aligned teams, letting them focus on business logic. The platform team exists to shrink the surface area of things product teams must understand.

questions.q: What is the 'golden path' (or 'paved road') in platform engineering vocabulary?
options: The recommended deployment sequence for blue-green releases with zero downtime

The set of opinionated, well-supported defaults the platform provides - a pre-configured combination of tools, templates, and workflows that represent the easiest and most recommended way to build, test, and deploy a service
The escalation path from a production incident to an engineering manager and CTO
A compliance checklist that all services must pass before receiving a production deployment approval
questions.explanation: The golden path (Netflix term) or paved road means: if you follow our recommended toolchain and templates, everything just works. It trades flexibility for speed and consistency. Teams can go off-path, but they lose platform support. The goal is to make the right way the easy way.

questions.q: What does 'you build it you run it' mean in a platform team context?
options: Each developer must personally deploy and monitor every service they write, with no assistance from SRE or ops teams

A DevOps operating model where the team that builds a service is also responsible for running it in production - including on-call duties and operational metrics - in contrast to the traditional hand-off to a separate operations team
A rule requiring all platform services to be built using infrastructure-as-code before they can be operated
An engineering policy that prohibits outsourcing any software component to third-party vendors
questions.explanation: 'You build it you run it' (Werner Vogels, Amazon) is a DevOps principle: product teams own their services end-to-end including production. Platform teams enable this by providing the operational tooling (observability, deployment automation) so teams can run their own services without needing a dedicated ops handoff.

questions.q: During a code review for this PR, Sarah (a member of the Platform Team) comments to David: 'This error response format is fantastic! It's exactly what we need - predictable and easy for developers to integrate. It really helps us offload some of the burden of handling errors from our consuming teams.' Considering Sarah's comment, which of the following best explains the Platform Team's role in this refactoring effort?
options: Focusing solely on technical performance metrics like API response time and throughput to ensure optimal system scalability.
Primarily ensuring compliance with strict security regulations regarding user data handling, regardless of the impact on developer experience.
Supporting developers by providing well-defined, self-service APIs with robust error handling and standardized responses, reducing their operational burden and promoting autonomy.
Managing all internal infrastructure dependencies for the user profile API to guarantee high availability and prevent outages - a purely reactive approach to problem resolution.

Options A, B, and C misrepresent the core function of a platform team-they are about enablement, not purely technical optimization, security compliance, or reactive infrastructure management.

exercises.subtitle: Practice API catalog vocabulary for developer portals: API listing, API consumer, deprecation in portal context, end-of-life APIs, subscribing to an API, and API key issuance.

questions.q: In a developer portal, what does 'subscribing to an API' typically mean?
options: Signing up for email newsletters about the API
Registering an application to use the API, which triggers API key issuance and grants access under the selected usage tier or plan
Following the API's social media account
Automatically receiving API changelog notifications
questions.explanation: In portal contexts, subscribing to an API means an API consumer (developer or application) registers for access - typically selecting a usage plan, receiving credentials, and gaining the right to call the API within defined limits.

questions.q: An API listing in a developer portal shows status: 'End-of-Life.' What should API consumers do?
options: Continue using the API as normal - 'end-of-life' is just a label
Migrate to a replacement API before the shutdown date, as no new features will be added and the API will eventually stop working
Contact support to extend the API's lifetime
Archive their application code
questions.explanation: 'End-of-Life' (EOL) means the API has been fully deprecated and a shutdown date has been or will be set. Consumers should migrate to the replacement API as soon as possible. The portal typically provides migration guides alongside EOL notices.

questions.q: What is an 'API consumer' in developer portal terminology?
options: A developer who reads API documentation without ever making calls
A developer, team, or application that actively calls the API - the primary audience the portal is designed to serve
A customer support agent who handles API-related complaints
An API that consumes another API's data
questions.explanation: An API consumer is any developer, application, or team that uses the API. Developer portals are designed around the consumer experience - making discovery, onboarding, and ongoing use as smooth as possible.

questions.q: A portal page says: 'Explore our APIs.' What is this page typically for?
options: A marketing page for non-technical executives
A browsable catalog where developers can discover available APIs, read their descriptions, view documentation, and initiate the subscription process
A page listing the company's API development team
A technical comparison of REST vs. GraphQL implementations
questions.explanation: 'Explore our APIs' is the entry point to the API catalog - a searchable, filterable listing of all available APIs with descriptions, versioning, status labels (active/deprecated), and links to documentation. It is the discovery interface for API consumers.

questions.q: What does 'API key issuance' refer to in a developer portal?
options: The physical printing of API documentation
The automated process by which the portal generates and delivers credentials (an API key or client ID/secret) to a developer after they subscribe to an API
The process of assigning version numbers to API releases
The approval workflow for enterprise API access
questions.explanation: API key issuance is the provisioning step after subscription - the portal generates unique credentials that the developer includes in API calls to authenticate. Portals typically allow developers to view, rotate, and revoke their keys.

questions.q: Reviewer: 'I'm seeing a lot of calls to the AuthService.validateToken() endpoint in this module. Are you sure we're handling rate limiting correctly? The API documentation specifies a maximum of 10 requests per minute for that endpoint, and I've noticed several exceeding that. What does the reviewer likely mean by 'rate limiting' in this context?
options: 'Rate limiting' refers to the overall cost of using the API, which is tracked through billing metrics.
'Rate limiting' describes a security mechanism that restricts the number of requests a user can make within a specific timeframe, preventing abuse and ensuring service stability.
'Rate limiting' is simply a technical term for error codes returned when too many requests are made.
'Rate limiting' dictates which developers have access to the API based on their historical usage.
questions.explanation: The reviewer is using 'rate limiting' precisely as it's defined in the API documentation - a mechanism to control the number of requests. It's not about overall cost or error codes; instead, rate limiting protects the API from being overloaded and ensures fair access for all consumers. Misconceptions often arise because 'rate limiting' is frequently used more broadly, but here it has a specific technical meaning related to request throttling.

questions.q: During a Slack discussion about API usage, a developer states: 'We need to implement throttling on the PaymentService API. The documentation explicitly limits requests per second to prevent overload.' What does 'throttling' refer to in this context regarding the PaymentService API?
options: A: Automatically rejecting all requests exceeding a defined limit, regardless of the request type.
B: Limiting the number of requests that can be processed within a specific timeframe (e.g., per second) to prevent service degradation.
C: Redirecting all requests to a backup server when the primary server reaches capacity.
D: Monitoring API usage patterns and dynamically adjusting response times based on demand.
questions.explanation: 'Throttling' in this scenario refers to limiting the rate at which requests are processed by an API. It's a crucial technique for managing resource constraints and preventing overload - as indicated by the developer's statement about 'explicit limits.' Options A and C represent more drastic measures than throttling, while option D describes another related concept: dynamic scaling.

options: different prices depending on the amount of data consumed
a discount offered for bulk purchases of API credits
questions.explanation: A tiered pricing model in APIs means that the cost varies based on consumption. This is common practice; users pay more as they use more of the API's resources (e.g., data volume or number of requests). The other options describe alternative pricing structures like fixed fees or unlimited access.

questions.q: A PR description reads: 'This change implements pagination for the Products API response. We're using the `page_size` and `page_number` parameters to control the number of products returned per request.' What is the primary benefit of using 'pagination' in an API?
options: to break up large datasets into smaller, more manageable chunks
to automatically throttle API requests based on user activity
questions.explanation: Pagination is a technique used to handle large datasets efficiently. By dividing the data into pages and using parameters like `page_size` and `page_number`, you can avoid overwhelming clients with massive responses and improve performance. This allows for smoother data retrieval and reduces bandwidth usage.

exercises.title: Portal Governance Vocabulary
exercises.subtitle: 5 exercises - practice the vocabulary for developer portal governance, entity ownership, catalog completeness, and metadata SLAs.

questions.q: Your platform team reports: "Twelve catalog entries have no owner - they are stale entries." What is a stale entry in a developer portal?
options: A catalog entry for a service that is currently down or failing health checks.
A catalog entry that has not been updated, verified, or claimed by a team - its metadata may be outdated or the service may no longer exist.
An entry that has been deprecated but remains visible for historical reference.
A draft entry that has been created but not yet published to the catalog.
questions.explanation: A stale entry is a catalog record that has decayed - the owning team may have disbanded, the service may have been decommissioned, or the metadata was never kept up to date. Stale entries reduce catalog trustworthiness. Governance processes typically include a stale entry SLA (e.g., "entries not verified in 90 days trigger an owner notification").

questions.q: A platform engineer says: "Our catalog completeness score is 64%." What does this metric measure?
options: The proportion of catalog entries that have all required fields populated - owner, lifecycle stage, documentation link, and system membership.
The percentage of catalog API calls that return a 200 response.
The ratio of active services to deprecated services in the catalog.
The percentage of developers who have logged into the portal at least once.
questions.explanation: A catalog completeness score measures data quality - how many entries have all required fields filled in. A score of 64% means 36% of entries are missing at least one mandatory field. Platform teams use this metric to drive governance campaigns: "All components must have an owner, lifecycle, and docs link by Q3."

questions.q: Complete the platform governance SLA statement: "Any service registered in the catalog must have a designated _____ - a team or individual who is accountable for keeping the metadata accurate and responding to dependency questions."
options: maintainer
publisher
author
owner
questions.explanation: Owner is the standard term in developer portals and software catalogs. In Backstage, spec.owner references a Group or User entity. Entity ownership is the foundation of portal governance - without it, there is no accountability for accuracy, incident response, or decommissioning decisions.

questions.q: A portal governance policy states: "All catalog entries must meet the metadata SLA within 30 days of registration." What does SLA for portal metadata typically include?
options: A set of required fields and update frequency expectations - such as owner, lifecycle, description, and documentation link - that all registered services must satisfy within a defined timeframe.
A legal agreement governing the retention of service data in the portal.
A service-level agreement with vendors supplying the portal infrastructure.
An API response time commitment for the catalog query endpoint.
questions.explanation: A metadata SLA defines the quality and freshness standards for catalog entries. It typically specifies: required fields (owner, lifecycle, system), optional fields (tags, links), and a time window for compliance after registration. Platform teams use automated scoring and reminders to enforce it. The SLA turns the catalog from a snapshot into a living record.

questions.q: Which statement best describes portal governance in the context of an internal developer portal?
options: The set of policies, processes, and metrics that ensure the developer portal's content remains accurate, owned, and useful - covering catalog quality, entry lifecycle, ownership assignment, and metadata standards.
The feature roadmap and release management process for the portal platform itself.
The access control rules that determine which developers can register new catalog entries.
The network security policies that control access to the portal's Kubernetes cluster.
questions.explanation: Portal governance is the operational discipline of keeping the developer portal trustworthy and useful over time. Without governance, catalogs decay: orphaned entries accumulate, metadata becomes stale, and developers stop trusting the portal. Good governance includes completeness scoring, stale entry detection, ownership validation, and regular review cycles.

questions.q: Sarah from the API team just posted this message in Slack: "I'm seeing a lot of requests hitting our /users/{userId} endpoint that are returning 404 errors. The documentation clearly states this endpoint should always be available, and we haven't made any recent changes to the underlying service."
options: A sudden increase in traffic to the endpoint is causing temporary overload, and the service is throttling requests.
Sarah should escalate the issue directly to the infrastructure team for investigation of potential outages.
The documentation is inaccurate and needs immediate updating.
This suggests a misconfiguration in a client application consuming the API - perhaps an incorrect URL or missing authentication headers. Sarah should investigate client-side issues first.

exercises.title: Developer Portal Onboarding Vocabulary Quiz
exercises.subtitle: Practice developer portal onboarding vocabulary: getting started guides, time to hello world, quickstart, sandbox environment, API key generation flow, and try-it console language.

questions.q: What is 'time to hello world' (TTFSC) as a developer experience metric?
options: The time it takes a developer to deploy a 'Hello World' application to production
The time from a developer first discovering the API to successfully making their first working API call - a key measure of onboarding friction
The time it takes to write a hello world program in the API's primary SDK language
The loading time of the portal's getting started page
questions.explanation: Time to Hello World (also called Time to First Successful Call) measures how quickly a new developer can make their first successful API call from scratch. It is the primary metric for developer onboarding experience quality.

questions.q: What is a 'sandbox environment' in a developer portal context?
options: A children's game section of the developer portal
A safe, isolated environment that mimics the production API but uses simulated data, allowing developers to test integrations without real transactions or charges
A staging environment used by the portal's own engineering team
A restricted environment where only approved partners can test
questions.explanation: A sandbox is a testing environment that behaves like production but uses mock data. Developers can make API calls, test edge cases, and experiment without affecting real users or incurring real costs - essential for safe exploration.

questions.q: A portal features 'try it in the console.' What does this typically allow developers to do?
options: Download the API's source code to their local console
Make live API calls directly from the browser within the documentation, without writing any code - to explore responses and test parameters immediately
Open a terminal emulator within the browser
Chat with the API's support team in a console interface
questions.explanation: An interactive 'try it' console (sometimes called an API explorer) lets developers make real or sandbox API calls from the browser by filling in parameters and clicking a button. It dramatically reduces the time to first successful call.

questions.q: What makes a 'quickstart' guide different from full API documentation?
options: A quickstart covers all API endpoints; full documentation covers only the main ones
A quickstart is focused, minimal, and opinionated - it gets a developer to a working example as fast as possible, skipping options and edge cases
A quickstart is only for enterprise customers; documentation is for all users
A quickstart is auto-generated; full documentation is written by hand
questions.explanation: A quickstart sacrifices completeness for speed. It makes opinionated choices (one language, one use case, one flow) and guides the developer to a working result in minutes. Full documentation covers all options; the quickstart covers the happy path.

questions.q: What is the purpose of an 'API key generation flow' in developer onboarding?
options: To teach developers how API keys are cryptographically generated
To guide a developer through creating an account, creating an application, and obtaining credentials - the essential steps before making any authenticated API call
To automatically rotate API keys on a schedule
To evaluate a developer's security knowledge before granting access
questions.explanation: The API key generation flow is the credential provisioning part of onboarding: sign up, create an app or project, and receive an API key. Portals that streamline this flow (fewer steps, clear instructions) reduce onboarding drop-off significantly.

questions.q: Sarah : "Hey team, I've just submitted a PR to integrate the new payment gateway. It's passing all tests locally, but I'm seeing intermittent failures in the staging environment - specifically, some users are getting a 'transaction declined' error. The logs show a 500 status code from the API endpoint. Can anyone take a look?" As a developer discussing this issue with Sarah, which of the following phrases best describes the next step you should suggest to investigate?
options: insufficient - the error rate is below 1% and the client reports no issues.
requesting immediate deployment to production to quickly resolve the problem.
asking her to double-check the API key configuration in the PR itself, as a common cause of this issue.
suggesting she examine the API response headers for more details about the error-particularly any correlation with user data or transaction IDs.
questions.explanation: The question highlights an intermittent staging environment problem. While deployment might seem tempting, it's crucial to diagnose the root cause before pushing changes live. Examining the API response headers is a standard debugging technique in API development; specifically looking for error codes and user-specific data can pinpoint issues like authentication problems or rate limiting. Option B is incorrect because immediate production deployment without investigation could exacerbate the problem, and option A suggests ignoring potential underlying issues simply due to a low error rate.

questions.q: David : "I've just created a PR to update the user authentication service. I've added comprehensive unit tests and integration tests, but during code review, John commented that 'the response from the /users endpoint isn't consistently returning JSON - sometimes it's plain text.' What is the most effective way for you to address this feedback within the PR discussion?
options: insufficient - the response headers are correctly configured.
request John to provide a specific example of the problematic response.
immediately modify the endpoint code to always return JSON, regardless of the input.
ask John for more details about the circumstances under which he observed the issue.
questions.explanation: The key here is understanding that 'inconsistent' feedback requires further investigation. Simply stating the response headers are configured correctly doesn't address the core problem - the *content* of the response isn't what it should be. Requesting a specific example from John allows you to reproduce and diagnose the issue directly. Option A is incorrect because blindly ensuring JSON output won't solve the underlying cause, and option C ignores the feedback entirely.

questions.q: Mark: "Just merged the new analytics dashboard. It's pulling data from the Events API and displaying it in real time. I've included a comment in the PR describing the changes and linking to the relevant documentation. Should I also create a separate ticket detailing the performance metrics we're tracking?"
options: Insufficient - Mark should focus solely on ensuring the dashboard functionality is working correctly before addressing performance.
Correct - Mark should proactively document performance metrics alongside functional changes to facilitate monitoring and troubleshooting, as this is standard practice for API integrations.
Incorrect - Creating a separate ticket is unnecessary; all relevant information is already contained within the PR description and documentation links.
Potentially correct-Mark should create a separate ticket *only if* the performance metrics are critical to business decisions and require immediate attention.
questions.explanation: This scenario highlights the importance of proactive monitoring in API integrations . Simply merging a PR with functional changes isn't enough; developers need to anticipate potential issues like performance bottlenecks. Creating a separate ticket focusing on metrics allows for focused tracking and facilitates collaboration if problems arise-it's a standard practice that aligns with DevOps principles and ensures ongoing visibility into the system's health. Option A is too restrictive, and option C misunderstands the purpose of PRs.

questions.q: Reviewer : "I'm seeing a lot of requests to the /metrics endpoint from mobile devices. The response times are consistently high - averaging around 800ms. Should we investigate this further?" As a developer responding to Reviewer , which statement best describes your immediate next action within the PR discussion?
options: Insufficient - the API response size is likely the bottleneck.
Request detailed logs from the mobile devices to identify potential errors or slow queries.
Immediately deploy a new version of the /metrics endpoint with optimized caching.
Ignore the feedback; high latency on non-critical endpoints is often acceptable.
questions.explanation: The key here isn't about immediately deploying changes or optimizing without understanding the root cause. A high response time for a metric endpoint from mobile devices strongly suggests a problem with the data retrieval process itself. Requesting detailed logs allows you to pinpoint whether the issue is slow queries on the backend, inefficient data aggregation, or network latency - providing valuable diagnostic information before attempting any optimizations which could mask the underlying problem. Option A is misleading as response size isn't the primary cause of high latency; option C is premature optimization without investigation, and option D is unacceptable given the severity of the performance issue.

exercises.title: Scorecard and Governance Vocabulary Quiz
exercises.subtitle: Practice scorecard and governance vocabulary: production readiness scorecards, service maturity models, compliance gates, ownership requirements, and runbook mandates.

questions.q: A platform team says 'the service has a score of 7/10 on the production readiness scorecard.' What does this mean?
options: The service passed 7 out of 10 unit tests
The service meets 7 of the 10 defined criteria for production readiness - such as having a runbook, defined SLOs, on-call coverage, and alerts configured
The service has a 70% uptime record
The service has 7 out of 10 API endpoints documented
questions.explanation: A production readiness scorecard evaluates services against defined criteria. A score of 7/10 means the service meets most requirements but has gaps. Teams use scorecards to systematically improve service quality before and after going to production.

questions.q: What are 'compliance gates' in a software delivery context?
options: Physical security gates in a data center
Automated or manual checks that a service must pass before progressing to the next stage - for example, requiring a security review before production deployment
Legal compliance forms that must be signed before code is shipped
Database transaction gates that ensure data compliance
questions.explanation: Compliance gates are checkpoints in the delivery pipeline that enforce governance requirements - such as security scans, license checks, or mandatory reviews. Services that fail a gate cannot proceed until the issue is resolved.

questions.q: A platform engineer says 'ownership is required for production.' What does this mean?
options: The company must own the server hardware to run production services
Every service in production must have a clearly defined team or individual owner registered in the service catalog, accountable for its reliability and incidents
Developers must own company stock to deploy to production
Services must be open-source to run in production
questions.explanation: 'Ownership is required for production' is a governance policy meaning every production service must have a registered owner - typically a team - who is accountable for on-call, incidents, and maintaining the service. Unowned services cannot go to production.

questions.q: What is a 'maturity model' in the context of service or platform governance?
options: A model that predicts when a software project will be ready to release
A framework that defines progressive levels of capability and quality - from basic to advanced - that a service or team works through to improve over time
A model describing the technical maturity needed for promotion to senior engineer
A security maturity assessment framework like CMMC
questions.explanation: A maturity model describes levels of practice quality - from ad hoc (Level 1) through managed and optimized (Level 4/5). Platform teams use maturity models to help service teams improve practices incrementally rather than requiring perfection immediately.

questions.q: A governance policy states 'this service needs a runbook.' What is a runbook?
options: A log of all code commits made to the service repository
A documented set of procedures for operating, troubleshooting, and responding to incidents for a specific service - essential for on-call engineers
A book of all API endpoints the service exposes
A project planning document for running the service's development roadmap
questions.explanation: A runbook is operational documentation: step-by-step procedures for common operational tasks and incident response scenarios. A service without a runbook makes on-call work much harder and is a common production readiness requirement.

questions.q: PR #1234 is in review. The lead reviewer comments: 'This feature introduces a potential performance bottleneck. We need to ensure the API response time doesn't exceed 500ms under peak load, as defined by our Service Level Objectives (SLOs). Consider adding caching or optimizing the database query.' What does the reviewer *primarily* mean when referring to 'Service Level Objectives (SLOs)' in this context?
options: A: SLOs are a list of technical tasks that need to be completed for this PR.
B: SLOs are specific, measurable goals relating to the performance and availability of the service, like response time or error rate.
C: SLOs represent the budget allocated for testing this new feature.
D: SLOs are guidelines for naming conventions within the codebase.
questions.explanation: The reviewer is focusing on quantifiable targets-response time and error rates-that define the desired behavior of the service. SLOs (Service Level Objectives) are formally agreed-upon metrics used to measure a service's performance and reliability. Options A, C, and D misinterpret SLOs; they relate to tasks, budget, or naming conventions respectively, not the core concept of measurable performance goals.

questions.q: PR #5678 is awaiting approval. A member of the platform team writes in the PR description: 'We're flagging this component for increased scrutiny due to its reliance on a third-party API. While the API itself has a 99.9% uptime SLA, we need to establish clear mitigation strategies if it experiences downtime-specifically, outlining steps for failover and alerting.' What does the team *primarily* intend when they refer to 'mitigation strategies' in this scenario?
questions.explanation: The team is concerned about potential downtime of a dependent service (the third-party API) despite its advertised SLA. 'Mitigation strategies' in this context refers to proactive actions - a documented plan - that would be executed if the primary API fails. Options A and D represent reactive approaches that don't address the core issue of dependency failure, while option C is insufficient as monitoring alone doesn't guarantee functionality during an outage.

questions.q: PR #9012 is awaiting merge. The engineering manager asks during a standup update: 'Can we get some data on the current score for this microservice on the governance scorecard? We need to understand if it's meeting our targets.' What does he *primarily* want to know when asking about the 'governance scorecard' in this situation?
options: The exact number of lines of code in the service.
A detailed breakdown of all the technical debt associated with the microservice.
An overall assessment of the service's adherence to defined policies and standards, often reflecting its stability, performance, and security posture.
The current sprint velocity for the development team working on the microservice.
questions.explanation: The manager isn't interested in technical details like code size or velocity. The governance scorecard is a tool used to evaluate services against established policies and standards - things like performance, security, reliability, and compliance. A high score indicates the service is meeting these requirements, while a low score would highlight areas needing improvement, triggering further investigation and potential corrective action. Therefore, an 'overall assessment' best captures what he's seeking.

questions.q: PR #7890 is awaiting approval. A team member writes in the PR description: 'We're implementing a new monitoring dashboard to track key metrics for this service. The dashboard will automatically alert us if response times exceed 2 seconds, or if error rates spike above 5%. We've defined these thresholds based on our Service Level Agreements (SLAs) and want to ensure proactive identification of potential issues.' What does the team *primarily* mean when referring to 'Service Level Agreements (SLAs)' in this scenario?
options: A: SLAs are legal contracts with users guaranteeing a specific level of service.
B: SLAs represent the agreed-upon performance targets for the service, including response times and error rates, which drive monitoring alerts.
C: SLAs dictate the technical architecture choices made during development to ensure optimal performance.
D: SLAs are only relevant during initial system testing and should be disregarded once the service is live.
questions.explanation: The team's discussion of 'Service Level Agreements (SLAs)' focuses on the *performance targets* for the service. SLAs formally define what's considered acceptable performance - in this case, response times and error rates - which directly trigger the monitoring alerts described. The incorrect options misunderstand the role of SLAs as legal contracts, architectural specifications, or irrelevant after deployment. This is a critical aspect of proactive governance.
